1324.title: the breath again — every claim checked
1324.hook: Patanjali's word for good breathing practice isn't strong or deep: it's long and subtle
1324.carry: the breath again — every claim checked
1324.tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked
1324.howItsDone: In yoga traditions that follow Patanjali, pranayama is practiced seated after posture practice, usually under a teacher, and the Yoga Sutras ask for a steady, easy seat before it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: a student asked too much, and the teacher drew breath as a king sending officers out to the villages.

Before the breath, a seat. In the Yoga Sutras, Patanjali says nothing about breathing practice until the body has somewhere steady to rest: posture first, then breath, in that order. A video promising a breathing hack can skip all that. Stand up, breathe hard, push through a number of rounds, collect a big promise. Today: the short run of sutras where Patanjali defines the practice, and one popular claim checked against them, that pranayama means pushing the breath as hard as you can.
screen: `BEFORE THE BREATH, A SEAT.` → `NOT LOUD, NOT FAST.` → `PATANJALI'S OWN DEFINITION.`

segments.voice: Start with the seat. Patanjali asks for a posture that is steady and easy, sthira and sukha. It comes, he says, as effort loosens and the mind rests on the endless. Only once that seat is there does pranayama come. Breath practice isn't the opening move; it rests on a body already settled. Then the definition, in paraphrase: pranayama is a pause in the flow of breathing in and breathing out. Not more breath. A gap in the movement. A few days ago came the sutra after that one: breath watched by place, time and count grows long and subtle. Look further on, at the fruit Patanjali names. A covering over the inner light thins, he says, and the mind becomes fit for concentration, ready to hold one thing. Now the claim: pranayama as maximum effort, gasping rounds, the harder the better. The Sutras don't say that. They say seated first, unforced, watched closely. That doesn't settle every question about every breathing method taught today, and the Sutras don't try to. It just means a hard, forceful practice can't borrow Patanjali's name for its intensity. One plain word to add: anyone with heart or lung trouble, or who gets dizzy, keeps breathing practice gentle and asks a doctor first. That isn't a modern caution laid over the text. It's the text's own spirit: a settled seat, and nothing forced.
screen: `A STEADY, EASY SEAT` · `A PAUSE IN THE FLOW` · `A MIND FIT FOR CONCENTRATION` · `NOT A PUSH`

segments.voice: Let the body settle until it's steady, then until it's easy: shoulders down, jaw loose, hands resting, effort loosening a little with each breath out. Only then turn to the breath, and don't steer it; if a natural little pause comes after a breath out, notice it without stretching it, and if anything strains, go back to the seat. If you pray, you can let the stillness be your prayer.
The breath again. In Patanjali, a steady, easy seat comes first, and pranayama is a pause in the flow of breath, not a push. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. Steady first, then easy, and only then the breath. See you tomorrow.

1325.title: the breath again — every claim checked
1325.hook: a yoga manual compares breath to a lion, an elephant and a tiger, and makes a promise worth checking
1325.carry: the breath again — every claim checked
1325.tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked
1325.howItsDone: In hatha yoga lineages, breath practices are traditionally learned gradually from a teacher, and the Hatha Yoga Pradipika itself warns that rushing them can cause harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: Patanjali puts a steady, easy seat first, and only then the breath.

A lion. An elephant. A tiger. Nobody tames one in an afternoon. A keeper works slowly, day after day, and even then stays careful. That's the picture a yoga manual called the Hatha Yoga Pradipika uses for the breath: it is to be brought under control the way those animals are, gradually. Then the same passage makes a promise and a warning side by side. This season promised to check every claim, and that includes the claims an old text makes about itself. Today: the tamed lion, and a promise held up to the light.
screen: `A LION, AN ELEPHANT, A TIGER.` → `SLOWLY, DAY AFTER DAY.` → `A PROMISE AND A WARNING.`

segments.voice: First the image, in paraphrase. As a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed little by little, so the breath is controlled little by little. Otherwise, the text says, it harms the one who practices. That's blunt: a yoga manual telling its readers that breath practice done carelessly can hurt them. Next, the promise and the warning in one verse. Done properly, the practice puts an end to disease. Done improperly, it brings disease on. Then it lists what can go wrong: hiccups, breathing trouble, cough, pain in the head, the ears and the eyes. So, every claim checked, this one too. The warning holds up well. Slow, gradual, careful is plain good sense for anyone trying a breathing practice, and these days hold to the same. The promise is a different matter. A claim that any practice ends every disease is one this path won't accept from any source, old or new. It's fair to say that clearly, and fair to say what the text is doing: it's a teaching manual, urging its students toward patience by showing them both what they hope for and what they risk. The respectful reading takes the text seriously and still checks it. Keep the lion and the slowness. Leave the cure-all on the page. And notice how human the passage is. Its author knew students would rush, so it sends them to the animal keeper, who never hurries a tiger.
screen: `TAMED LITTLE BY LITTLE` · `A PROMISE AND A WARNING IN ONE VERSE` · `THE WARNING HOLDS UP` · `THE CURE-ALL STAYS ON THE PAGE`

segments.voice: Tame nothing today; just befriend. Let the breath move on its own and watch its pace, the way a keeper watches an animal before ever reaching out a hand: quick if it wants to be quick, slow if it slows, and if anything strains, back to ordinary breathing. If you pray, you can hold one breath of thanks.
The breath again. In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, breath is tamed little by little, like a lion, an elephant or a tiger. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. Slow is the old word on breath, and still a good one. Rest well.

1326.title: the breath again — every claim checked
1326.hook: in the Gita's list of offerings, some people offer their breath, and it sits in a row with everyone else's gift
1326.carry: the breath again — every claim checked
1326.tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked
1326.howItsDone: Some Hindus treat daily actions, breathing among them, as offerings in the spirit of the Gita's fourth chapter, and the Gita's verses on breath are recited and studied in traditions of yoga.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: a yoga manual said breath is tamed like a lion, slowly. Its caution stayed, and its promise got checked.

What would it mean to give a breath away? Not to hold it, or push it, or count it. To offer it, the way a person sets a flower down in front of an image or pours a spoon of ghee into a fire. In the fourth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna walks Arjuna through a long list of offerings people make. Wealth, study, discipline, the restraint of the senses. And in the middle of the list, quietly, breath. Today: what the Gita does with the breath, and a claim about it that the list itself answers.
screen: `GIVE A BREATH AWAY?` → `A LIST OF OFFERINGS.` → `BREATH, IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Some, Krishna says, offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath, holding the path of both, given over to the practice of breath. The breath going in is poured into the breath going out, like an offering into a fire, and back again. Breathing itself becomes a yajna, a sacrifice. The ordinary thing the body does all day is treated as a gift. Then look at the company it keeps. Some offer their senses into the fire of restraint. Some offer their possessions. Some offer austerity, some study, some yoga. And a short line sums up the whole row: all of these know what sacrifice is. Now the claim. You'll sometimes hear that the Gita names breath control as the highest yoga, the secret above all others. Check it against the chapter. Breath is there, honored, given its own careful verse. But it stands in a row with study, with giving, with self-restraint. The list doesn't crown it. What the Gita adds is a direction: the point of the breath isn't what you get from it, but what you give with it. Later, in the fifth chapter, the Gita mentions making the in-breath and out-breath even as they move within the nostrils, and there too breath serves a larger aim: a person free of desire, fear and anger. So the claim shrinks, and the teaching grows. In the Gita, breath can be an offering.
screen: `IN-BREATH POURED INTO OUT-BREATH` · `BREATHING AS A SACRIFICE` · `ONE GIFT IN A ROW OF GIFTS` · `NOT WHAT YOU GET, BUT WHAT YOU GIVE`

segments.voice: Notice the breath in arriving and let it flow into the breath out without a seam, then the breath out turning into the breath in, like the gentlest offering: something set down, not thrown. If you pray, you can offer your breathing, just as it is, to God, as some Hindus do; if you don't, you can simply let it go with thanks.
The breath again. In the Gita, some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, one gift in a row of many. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. One ordinary breath, set down as a gift. See you tomorrow.

1327.title: the breath again — every claim checked
1327.hook: a son keeps bringing his father an answer, and the father keeps sending him back, past food, past breath
1327.carry: the breath again — every claim checked
1327.howItsDone: The Taittiriya Upanishad's story of Bhrigu is studied in Vedanta as a teaching on the layers of a person, food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss, and is also chanted in Vedic recitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: in the Gita, some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, one gift in a row of gifts.

Breath is Brahman. That's the second answer a young man named Bhrigu brings home to his father, Varuna, in the third part of the Taittiriya Upanishad. This path met him over food, his first answer. The clue hasn't changed: Brahman is that from which beings are born, by which they live, and into which they return. Go and practice, and find out. Food fit the clue, and still he was sent out again. Now he's back with breath. On the last day of a season built on checking claims: the step after food, and what the Upanishad says breath is.
screen: `BREATH IS BRAHMAN.` → `THE SECOND ANSWER.` → `ONE HONEST ANSWER AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's how the second answer comes, in paraphrase. Bhrigu practices again, and comes to see that breath is Brahman. From breath beings are born, by breath they live, into breath they return. It fits the clue. The second part of the same Upanishad has a short verse that says why: the gods breathe along with breath, and so do people, and so do animals. Breath is the life of beings, so it's called the life of all. It names no technique. It promises no cure. It points at something plain enough to check against your own body: while there's life, there's breath. That claim grew when it was checked. And still Varuna says, practice again. Bhrigu goes on, to mind, to understanding, and at last to bliss, and this time he isn't sent away. A fitting shape for closing this season on Ayurveda as a lens: the doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis; the day's rhythm, the seasons, food, sleep; and these last days, breath, with every claim given a label: the text says, tradition says, a doctor decides. Breath as the power the senses follow, a king sending out officers, a steady seat, a lion tamed slowly, an offering. Some claims grew when checked, and some shrank. Bhrigu's way sits under all of it: bring an answer, test it against the clue, keep what holds, and stay willing to be sent out again.
screen: `BREATH IS BRAHMAN` · `BREATH IS THE LIFE OF BEINGS` · `MIND, UNDERSTANDING, THEN BLISS` · `KEEP WHAT HOLDS, LOOK FURTHER`

segments.voice: Climb Bhrigu's steps slowly: notice the body, the food that built it, the weight on the seat; then the breath, coming and going on its own; then the mind, thoughts arriving and leaving; then the knowing that is aware of all of it. Then simply rest, and let whatever ease is there be enough. If you pray, you can rest in God's presence.
The breath again. In the Taittiriya, Bhrigu finds that breath is Brahman, and his father sends him on, past breath, to look further. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. Tomorrow, a new season: the women of the epics, starting with Sita. Until tomorrow.

1328.title: Sita
1328.hook: a king is plowing a field, and a girl rises out of the furrow
1328.howItsDone: Sita is honored in Hindu devotion as a goddess and as Rama's wife, and her birth is celebrated in some communities as Sita Navami; her story is retold in Valmiki's Ramayana and in later versions such as Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a season with the breath again: Bhrigu found that breath is Brahman, and his father sent him on to look further.

A king is plowing. Not a farmer, a king, walking behind the plow, clearing a field. And out of the furrow, out of the turned earth, a girl rises. He lifts her up, takes her home, and raises her as his own daughter. The king is Janaka of Mithila. The girl is Sita. A new season starts today: the women of the epics, heard in their own words where the texts give them words. It starts with the one who came out of the ground.
screen: `A KING BEHIND THE PLOW.` → `A GIRL RISES FROM THE FURROW.` → `A SEASON OF THE EPICS' WOMEN.`

segments.voice: The story comes late in the first book of Valmiki's Ramayana, from Janaka's own mouth. In paraphrase: while I was plowing the field, a girl rose from the earth. I found her while clearing the ground, and she is known by the name Sita. She was not born from a womb, he adds, and he calls her his daughter. Then he sets a test for any man who wants to marry her: lift and string the great bow of Shiva that sits in his house. Many have tried, he says, and failed. In the next chapter, Rama lifts the bow, and it breaks. Three things to hold as this season begins. First, the name. Tradition hears in it the Sanskrit word for a furrow, the line the plow cuts, so her name carries the field she came from. Second, her father. The Upanishads tell of a King Janaka who loved to ask about the self, the one heard earlier on this path questioning Yajnavalkya about dreams and deep sleep, and tradition links Sita's father to that king or to his line. In that telling, the girl from the furrow grows up in a house of seekers. Third, the shape of her story. She comes out of the earth here, at the start. In the Ramayana's last book, she goes back into it: the ground opens and takes her home. The season ahead isn't about who Sita belongs to. It's about what she says and chooses, where the text lets her speak.
screen: `JANAKA TELLS IT IN HIS OWN WORDS` · `THE BOW OF SHIVA` · `A NAME THAT CARRIES THE FIELD` · `FROM THE EARTH, AND BACK TO IT`

segments.voice: Let your weight drop and notice exactly where the floor or the earth meets you, the feet, the seat, the hands, settling a little more with each breath out onto the same ground that was under Sita, turned, planted, walked on. If you pray, you can give thanks for the earth, as some Hindus do when they touch it in the morning; otherwise, simply rest on it.
Sita. In Valmiki, Janaka finds her rising from the earth as he plows, and tradition hears the furrow in her name. Today's word.
Your line: Sita. From the furrow at the start, and back to the earth at the end. Same time tomorrow.

1329.title: Sita
1329.hook: Rama tells Sita to stay home while he goes into exile, and she argues, and wins
1329.howItsDone: Sita's choice to follow Rama into exile is retold in Ramayana recitations and Ram Lila performances, and Hindu teachers read it both as a model of devotion and as a scene of her own strong will.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita: a girl rising out of the furrow as King Janaka plowed, her name the line the plow cuts.

I will walk ahead of you. That, in paraphrase, is Sita's answer when Rama comes to tell her he's been sent into the forest, and that she should stay behind. The crown he was promised has been taken away. He's leaving soon. He has a careful speech ready about how she should live in Ayodhya while he's gone: honor his parents, don't praise him in front of the new heir. Sita doesn't take the speech. She takes the floor. Today: the argument in Valmiki's second book, where Sita's own words decide where she goes.
screen: `I WILL WALK AHEAD OF YOU.` → `A CAREFUL SPEECH, REFUSED.` → `SITA'S OWN WORDS DECIDE.`

segments.voice: She starts with a reason. A father, a mother, a brother, a son, she says, each lives by their own lot. A wife shares her husband's. If he is sent to the forest, so is she. Then she gets practical. I'll go first, and tread down the thorns and the sharp grass on the path. The forest with you is better to me than any palace without you. Rama tries again. He describes the forest honestly: wild animals, cold, hunger, sleeping on the ground. It's no place for you, he says. And here the text lets Sita get angry. In paraphrase: what was my father thinking, she asks, when he took you as a son-in-law? Did he think you were a man, when you're a woman in a man's form? It's a sharp line, and Valmiki keeps it. Then she weeps, and holds him, and Rama gives way. Come, he says. The Sita of this chapter is not quiet. She argues from duty, from love and from plain stubbornness, and she wins. Some readers hear devotion here first: a wife who will not be parted from her husband. Others hear a woman choosing her own road against the man trying to choose it for her. The text holds both, and gives her the words either way. The thorns she promises to tread down are hers to tread.
screen: `A WIFE SHARES HER HUSBAND'S LOT` · `I'LL TREAD DOWN THE THORNS` · `A WOMAN IN A MAN'S FORM?` · `DEVOTION, AND HER OWN ROAD`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one road ahead of you, a hard conversation, a move, a long week, and let someone you love come to mind alongside it. Ask quietly whether there's a thorn on that path you could tread down first, for them, and don't plan it; just breathe with whatever shows itself. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.
Sita. In Valmiki's second book, she refuses to stay behind, argues with Rama, and walks into exile at his side. Today's word.
Your line: Sita. The forest with him, over any palace without him. See you tomorrow.

1330.title: Sita
1330.hook: a captive in a grove puts a blade of grass between herself and a king, and later turns down her own rescue
1330.howItsDone: The Sundara Kanda, the book of Hanuman's journey and Sita in the grove, is recited on its own by some Hindus as a devotional reading, and Sita in the ashoka grove is a familiar scene in temple art and Ram Lila.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita: told to stay behind, she argued, promised to tread down the thorns, and walked into exile beside Rama.

A single blade of grass. In Valmiki's fifth book, the Sundara Kanda, that's what Sita sets down between herself and Ravana. She's a captive in his city of Lanka, kept in a grove of ashoka trees, guarded day and night. He comes to her with jewels, promises and threats. She doesn't look at him. She picks up a blade of grass, places it between them, and speaks to the grass. Today: two choices Sita makes in the grove, both in her own words, and the second is a no to the one who has come to find her.
screen: `A SINGLE BLADE OF GRASS.` → `A CAPTIVE IN THE ASHOKA GROVE.` → `TWO CHOICES, IN HER OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: The first choice is the grass. Ravana offers her his kingdom, and his queens as her servants. Sita answers through the blade of grass, in paraphrase: turn your mind back to your own wives. I am not for you, the way the light is not for anyone but the sun. Give me back to Rama, if you want to live. The grass is a wall made of almost nothing. It says: I won't even speak to you face to face. The second choice comes later, and it's stranger. Hanuman, Rama's messenger, slips into the grove and shows her Rama's ring, so she knows he's real. Then he makes the obvious offer: climb on my back, and I'll carry you across the sea tonight. Sita says no, and the text keeps her reasons. You might drop me over the water, or be attacked while carrying me. I won't willingly touch the body of any man but Rama. And this is Rama's to finish: let him come, defeat Ravana, and take me back himself, as a hero should. Then she gives Hanuman a jewel from her hair and a private memory from the forest, so Rama will know the message is truly from her. Sita is the captive, and she is still the one choosing. She sets the terms of her own conversation with Ravana, and the terms of her own rescue. Valmiki could have written a woman simply waiting. He wrote one who keeps deciding.
screen: `SHE SPEAKS THROUGH A BLADE OF GRASS` · `THE RING, AND THE OFFER OF A RIDE` · `SITA SAYS NO, AND GIVES REASONS` · `THE CAPTIVE KEEPS DECIDING`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that keeps pressing on you, a voice, a habit, a worry, and instead of fighting it, picture a single blade of grass set down between you and it. Breathe on your side of that small, quiet boundary, and notice that you can still choose where your attention goes. If you pray, you can hold that space before God.
Sita. In the ashoka grove, she speaks to Ravana through a blade of grass and turns down Hanuman's offer to carry her home. Today's word.
Your line: Sita. A blade of grass can be a wall. Rest well.
